extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of constitutional law and political science; statesmen and informed readers interested in government structure
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of the structure, powers, and practical effects of a federal constitution, comparing federal and monarchical systems and assessing institutional tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a single national head for external relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The external relations of a people cannot be advantageously maintained without the agency of a single head of a Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive national prerogatives should include the right of making peace and war, concluding treaties of commerce, raising armies, and equipping fleets (see Constitution, sect. 8; Federalist Nos. 41–42). A single head is required to manage relations with other nations effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal control over certain general internal interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain general interests can only be attended to with advantage by a general authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Union should control the monetary system, direct the post office, and open great roads to establish communication between regions. Other analogous privileges include legislating on bankruptcy and granting patents—matters where national intervention is clearly necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited and predetermined federal interference in state internal affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Government is authorized to interfere in the internal affairs of the States only in a few predetermined cases to protect the security of the Union at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in those cases interference is largely indirect (for example, via tribunals). States retain broad legislative power (may modify and change their legislation), but are forbidden to enact ex post facto laws or create a class of nobles (Federal Constitution, sect. 10, art. I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal taxing power sufficient to fulfil national engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Government must be endowed with an unlimited power of levying taxes to be able to fulfil its engagements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal capacity is necessary for national commitments; without adequate taxing power the Union could not carry out its responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization in key respects (one tribunal and one legislature)
rubrics_metrics.description: In essential points the Union exercises more central authority than some European monarchies: there is one tribunal to interpret the law and one legislature to make the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An impost voted by the nation’s representatives is binding on all citizens—this centralization can exceed that of historical monarchies even though the Union is formally a confederation of republics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of legislative powers into two branches embodying different principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal legislature is divided into a Senate and a House of Representatives, reflecting two opposed principles: the independence of the States (Senate) and the sovereignty of the nation (House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each State sends two senators (state-equality principle) while representatives are apportioned by population (national-sovereignty principle). This compromise reconciles conflicting interests but can produce singular effects, such as minority influence in the Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral compromise as a pragmatic, not purely logical, solution
rubrics_metrics.description: When conflicting interests exist (state independence vs national sovereignty), a middle course (bicameral compromise) is adopted that evades strict logical consistency but balances practical concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because nations are heterogeneous and interests differ, constitutions often adopt compromises; the result may deviate from pure theory but can work in practice given demographic and cultural proximity among states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different modes of election, terms, and functions for each House
rubrics_metrics.description: Senators are named by state legislatures (double election) for six-year terms; Representatives are chosen directly by the people for two-year terms; their powers and functions differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The House’s functions are mainly legislative (and impeachment initiation); the Senate co-operates in legislation, tries impeachments, ratifies treaties, and confirms appointments (see Federalist Nos. 52–56; Constitution sects. 2–3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive should be elective, responsible, and independent within its sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is an elective magistrate who is responsible to the people, free to act in his own sphere under the inspection (but not direction) of the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To preserve republican government the executive must be subject to the nation’s will; yet it must also possess sufficient stability and strength (four-year term, re-eligibility) to act effectively. Salary is fixed at entry to protect independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspensive veto as an executive check and appeal mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The President’s suspensive veto allows him to oppose laws, forcing reconsideration and, if persisted in by the legislature, requiring a two-thirds majority to override.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The veto operates as an appeal to the people and protects executive independence by compelling legislative reconsideration; it does not make the executive supreme but provides a procedural check.

rubrics_metrics.name: President as executor, not co-legislator (contrast with constitutional monarch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike a constitutional King who shares in law formation and can influence the legislature’s composition, the President is primarily the executor of laws and has no right to dissolve or directly form the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The King may appoint members of a chamber or dissolve assemblies; the President cannot, and his ministers are excluded from Congress, so his influence must be indirect. This structural difference makes the President’s authority inferior to that of a constitutional monarch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration (tenure) of office affects executive power and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparatively short, elective tenure of a President (four years) weakens the office relative to hereditary monarchs, for whom duration is a key element of strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Durability fosters respect and continuous action; elective, short-term executives face instability and limited personal authority compared with long-tenured or hereditary sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances determine the practical scope of executive prerogatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The real influence of executive prerogatives depends on circumstances: external threats, size of armed forces, and geographic position influence how much of the President’s powers can be exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A weak army, few ships, and geographic isolation reduce occasions for exercising foreign-policy prerogatives; thus legal powers may exist but be unusable in practice, diminishing executive influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of the elective system scale with the extent of executive prerogatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The dangers inherent in electing a chief magistrate increase in proportion to the magnitude of the prerogatives vested in the office—the greater the power, the greater the temptation to ambition and faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before adopting an elective executive, evaluate geography, laws, habits, manners, and opinions of the people: elective sovereignty is workable where the executive’s sphere is circumscribed and the people accustomed to living without strong executive protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective system inevitably introduces instability; impact depends on executive strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections create periods of suspense and instability, which are more damaging when the executive wields broad authority; when executive power is small, as in the U.S., the disadvantage is less acute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elections divert incumbents, delay initiatives, and may leave government action slackened. The US case shows limited harm so long as most directing authority rests with representatives rather than the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive prerogative to select and remove agents enhances responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The head of the executive should be empowered to choose his own agents and remove them at pleasure; legislative bodies should watch conduct rather than directly control appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing the executive control over his agents strengthens accountability and coherent administration; however, as a consequence, each election places the fate of federal public officers in suspense.
